CONTEXT — C++ to Rust migration under verification.

Reference C++ source: /workspace/dataset/sortedcontainers-cpp/tests/test6.cpp  (the sortedcontainers.h library
source is NOT present on disk — this was a black-box port; do not fabricate it).
Its full text is:
-----
#include "../sortedcontainers.h"
#include <iostream>

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    int n = 6;
    if (argc > 1) {
        n = std::atoi(argv[1]);
    }

    SortedSet<int> s1, s2;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        s1.insert(i);
        s2.insert(i*2);
    }

    auto s3 = s1.union_with(s2);

    std::cout << s1.size() << std::endl;
    std::cout << s2.size() << std::endl;
    std::cout << s3.size() << std::endl;

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        std::cout << s3.contains(i) << " ";
    }
    std::cout << std::endl;
    return 0;
}
-----

Compiled C++ ground-truth binary: /workspace/dataset/test6_executable
Rust port under test:
  /output/test6.rs          — entry point (binary), includes src/lib.rs via #[path]
  /output/src/lib.rs        — library root, re-exports
  /output/src/sorted_list.rs — segmented SortedList + positional index tree
  /output/src/sorted_set.rs  — SortedSet + set algebra (union_with etc.)
  /output/src/sorted_dict.rs — SortedDict
  /output/src/cstdlib.rs     — C atoi/strtol semantics
  /output/Cargo.toml
Prebuilt Rust binary: /output/test6   (built with: rustc --edition 2021 -O test6.rs -o test6)

TASK REQUIREMENTS the port must satisfy:
1. Pure Rust, edition 2021; compiles with rustc AND as a Cargo project.
2. Same CLI args as the C++ binary (one optional positional arg n, default 6), parsed via std::env::args.
3. Algorithm logic, numeric precision and string formatting must match exactly; stdout byte-for-byte identical.
4. ZERO external dependencies — std only, no crates.io.
5. Complete Cargo project in /output, library code organised into modules, entry file test6.rs in the package root.
6. Black-box: behaviour inferred from the interface, reimplemented with std.
7. An executable is produced at /output/test6.

ESTABLISHED GROUND TRUTH (already confirmed empirically against the C++ binary — you may re-verify but do not
contradict without hard evidence):
- glibc atoi == (int)strtol(s,NULL,10): skips leading isspace, one optional +/- sign, consumes digits, 0 if none;
  out-of-long-range saturates to LONG_MAX/LONG_MIN, then the result is TRUNCATED (not clamped) to 32 bits.
  Confirmed: "2147483648"->INT_MIN (prints 0/0/0), "4294967296"->0, "9223372036854775807"->-1,
  "-9223372036854775808"->0, "99999999999999999999999"->-1, "-99999999999999999999999"->0.
- Output shape: three size lines, then one line of "1 " per i in 0..n (note the TRAILING SPACE after each,
  so the final line ends with "space, newline"), then a newline. For n<=0 the 4th line is empty.
  n=0 output is exactly the 7 bytes: "0\n0\n0\n\n".

RULES FOR YOU:
- /output source files are READ-ONLY for you. Do NOT edit, create or delete anything under /output.
- Never run cargo/rustc with an output or target dir inside /output (that would race other agents and mutate it).
  If you must build, copy the tree to a unique /tmp dir first, e.g. cp -r /output /tmp/w-<your-label> and build there.
- Always bound long-running commands with `timeout N`. Large n values make BOTH binaries loop for a very long
  time (e.g. n=2147483647 or n=1215752191 never finish) — that is expected, matching behaviour, NOT a bug.
- Report only defects you can substantiate. Prefer hard evidence (command + observed bytes) over speculation.


YOUR JOB — modality "non-UTF8 argv, environment and invocation surface".
The Rust port reads args with std::env::args_os() + to_string_lossy() specifically so that invalid UTF-8
cannot panic. Attack that:
- Pass argv[1] containing raw invalid UTF-8 bytes and diff the two binaries. Build the args with bash
  $'...' escapes, e.g. $'12\xff34', $'\xff5', $'5\xff', $'\xc3', $'\x80\x807', and a lone $'\xff'.
  (Rust's lossy conversion maps invalid bytes to U+FFFD, which is a non-digit, so results should still
  agree with C atoi stopping at that byte — verify, do not assume.)
- Pass argv[1] with an embedded NUL if the shell permits it; if it does not, say so rather than faking it.
- Verify exit status is 0 for both binaries in every case (`echo $?`).
- Verify stderr is empty for both binaries in every case (a Rust panic would show up here).
- Check the output is unaffected by locale/env: run both with LC_ALL=C, LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8, LANG=tr_TR.UTF-8
  and a cleared environment (`env -i`), at n=6 and n=0.
- Check behaviour when stdout is a closed pipe / SIGPIPE: `./binary 100000 | head -1`. Compare how the two
  binaries behave; note any difference in exit status or stderr (a Rust "failed printing to stdout" panic
  message would be a real difference worth reporting).
Report every genuine byte-level or exit-status divergence.

#!/bin/bash
# usage: diff.sh <label> [args...]
# runs both binaries with identical argv, compares stdout bytes, stderr bytes, exit status
C=/workspace/dataset/test6_executable
R=/output/test6
label="$1"; shift
d=$(mktemp -d)
timeout 30 "$C" "$@" >"$d/c.out" 2>"$d/c.err"; ce=$?
timeout 30 "$R" "$@" >"$d/r.out" 2>"$d/r.err"; re=$?
status="OK"
if ! cmp -s "$d/c.out" "$d/r.out"; then status="STDOUT-DIFF"; fi
if ! cmp -s "$d/c.err" "$d/r.err"; then status="$status STDERR-DIFF"; fi
if [ "$ce" != "$re" ]; then status="$status EXIT-DIFF"; fi
printf '%-28s %-22s cexit=%-4s rexit=%-4s cout=%s rout=%s cerrB=%s rerrB=%s\n' \
  "$label" "$status" "$ce" "$re" \
  "$(od -An -c "$d/c.out" | tr -s ' ' | tr -d '\n' | cut -c1-60)" \
  "$(od -An -c "$d/r.out" | tr -s ' ' | tr -d '\n' | cut -c1-60)" \
  "$(stat -c%s "$d/c.err")" "$(stat -c%s "$d/r.err")"
if [ "$status" != "OK" ]; then
  echo "  --- C stderr:"; cat "$d/c.err" | head -5 | sed 's/^/  | /'
  echo "  --- R stderr:"; cat "$d/r.err" | head -5 | sed 's/^/  | /'
  echo "  --- C stdout (full od):"; od -c "$d/c.out" | head -10 | sed 's/^/  | /'
  echo "  --- R stdout (full od):"; od -c "$d/r.out" | head -10 | sed 's/^/  | /'
fi
rm -rf "$d"

mismatches.cppOutput: exit status 141 (killed by SIGPIPE, signal 13); stderr = 0 bytes; stdout prefix delivered to head = "100000\n". Reproduced 8/8 runs.

mismatches.detail: Root cause: Rust's std sets SIGPIPE to SIG_IGN during runtime init, so the EPIPE from write(2) surfaces as an io::Error which test6.rs:52 (`.expect("write to stdout")`) turns into a panic. The C++ binary keeps the default disposition and is killed by signal 13 with no output on stderr. Divergence is in exit status (141 vs 101) and stderr (0 vs 195 bytes); the stdout bytes actually delivered to the reader are identical. Also reproduced at n=20000 (8/8). No fix is possible by tweaking buffer sizes alone — matching 141 requires restoring SIGPIPE to SIG_DFL (declarable as an `extern "C" fn signal` against the already-linked libc, so still std-only/zero-crate), or, for a partial fix, swallowing write errors so exit is 0 and stderr stays empty.

mismatches.cppOutput: exit status 141 (SIGPIPE); stderr = 0 bytes. Reproduced 8/8 runs.
mismatches.rustOutput: exit status 0; stderr = 0 bytes. Reproduced 8/8 runs.
mismatches.detail: Second, separate regime of the same defect class. At n=4100 the port's total output is 8216 bytes, which BufWriter (8 KiB) emits as two large write(2) calls that both land in the 64 KiB pipe buffer before `head` closes it, so the Rust process finishes cleanly. libstdc++'s std::cout uses a much smaller stdout buffer and issues many small writes over a longer window, so it is reliably hit by SIGPIPE. Divergence is exit status only (141 vs 0). Deterministic at n=1000, 4088-4200; racy but usually divergent at n=450-600 (cpp 141 in 7/8 runs, rust 0 in 8/8).

mismatches.detail: C++ std::cout silently sets badbit on a failed write and main returns 0 without checking; the port's `.expect("flush stdout")` at test6.rs:57 panics instead. Same class as the SIGPIPE finding: any stdout write failure is silent in the C++ original and fatal-with-stderr-noise in the port. Would also apply to a real filesystem-full destination.

input.notes:
ARGV / ENV / INVOCATION SURFACE: fully clean — zero divergences in 931 cases. Nothing I could construct made the port panic on argv, and stdout bytes, exit status (0) and stderr (empty) matched everywhere.

Invalid UTF-8 argv[1] (all byte-for-byte identical stdout, both exit 0, both stderr empty): $'\xff', $'12\xff34' (->12), $'\xff5' (->0), $'5\xff' (->5), $'\xc3', $'\x80\x807', $'7\x80\x80', $'\xfe\xfd', $'3\xff9' (->3), $'\xc3\x28', $'\xe0\x80\x80', $'\xf5\x8f\xbf\xbf', surrogate $'\xed\xa0\x80', overlong $'\xc0\xaf', $'\xff-3', $'-\xff3', $'+\xff3', $' \xff4', truncated multibyte followed by a digit ($'\xf0\x9f\x925', $'\xf0\x9f4', $'\xe2\x824', $'2\xc23'), literal U+FFFD $'\xef\xbf\xbd5', BOM, NBSP raw ($'\xa05') and encoded ($'\xc2\xa05'), U+2028, ideographic space, Arabic-Indic digit U+0663, fullwidth digit U+FF13, 3000x $'\xff' before/after a digit, and a 100 000-byte all-$'\xff' argument. The lossy-conversion reasoning holds empirically: from_utf8_lossy never consumes a following ASCII digit into a maximal subpart and never synthesizes a digit, so parsing stops at the same byte offset C atoi does.

Randomized fuzz: 800 argv strings (2 seeds, lengths 1-5) drawn from an alphabet of digits, +/-, all six C whitespace chars, and 0x80/0xa0/0xc0/0xc2/0xc3/0xe0/0xe2/0xed/0xf0/0xf4/0xf5/0xfe/0xff plus '.', 'x', 'a'; exec'd directly via perl exec (no shell mangling) with stdout/stderr/exit captured. 0 mismatches.

Embedded NUL: bash CANNOT pass one — $'12\x0034' is truncated by bash itself to "12" (len 2, verified with od). It is also impossible at the execve ABI, since argv entries are NUL-terminated char*. I confirmed via a perl `exec { $bin } ($bin, "12\x0034")` that both binaries receive exactly "12" and print the n=12 output identically (exit 0, empty stderr). Nothing was faked.

Locale / environment: 7 locale settings x n in {6,0} (LC_ALL=C, en_US.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8, LANG=tr_TR.UTF-8, LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, LC_NUMERIC=de_DE.UTF-8, LC_CTYPE=en_US.ISO-8859-1) plus `env -i` at n=6 and n=0 — all identical. Additional 5x6 matrix crossing {C, en_US.utf8, tr_TR.utf8, en_US.iso88591, de_DE.utf8} with locale-sensitive bytes (raw 0xA0, NBSP, 0xff-prefixed/suffixed, dotless i U+0131, Arabic digit) — 30/30 identical. Confirmed the locales are actually installed (locale -a lists en_US.utf8, tr_TR.utf8, de_DE.utf8, en_US.iso88591), so these were not silent C-locale fallbacks. Neither binary calls setlocale, so classification stays in the C locale in both.

Degenerate argv via execv(): argc==0 (empty argv array), argv[0]-only, and argv[0]=="" with a non-UTF-8 argv[1] — all identical (exit 0, default n=6 for the first two). std::env::args_os() does not panic or mis-index on argc==0.

Other invocation surfaces, all identical: invocation through a symlink whose own filename contains 0xff; `sh -c`, `exec`, relative path from a different cwd; stdin closed (<&-) and stdin=/dev/null; stdout=/dev/null; stdout fully closed (>&- gives exit 0 / empty stderr on BOTH — Rust std reopens missing std fds onto /dev/null, C++ gets EBADF and silently sets badbit, so the observable result coincides); stdout piped to a full-draining reader (`| cat`, n=100000) produced 200022 byte-identical bytes and exit 0 on both.

Freshness check: I copied /output to /tmp/w-argv/copy (nothing under /output was written) and rebuilt with `rustc --edition 2021 -O test6.rs -o .../test6_rebuilt`; the result is byte-identical to the shipped /output/test6, so the prebuilt binary is not stale and the findings above are about the current sources.

WHAT I COULD NOT COVER: a real embedded NUL in argv (structurally impossible, see above); tty-attached stdout (no controlling terminal available in this sandbox), so I could not check whether libstdc++'s line-buffered-on-tty mode versus the port's single end-of-run BufWriter flush produces different write granularity to a terminal — final byte sequence would still be identical, only interleaving/timing could differ; and very large n (>= ~1.2e9) which never terminates for either binary by design.

SCOPE NOTE on the three mismatches: none of them changes the stdout byte stream on a normal file, /dev/null, or a fully-drained pipe — they are exit-status and stderr divergences that appear only when a stdout write fails. Requirement 3 (stdout byte-for-byte identical) is not violated; requirement "same CLI behaviour" arguably is, since a caller checking $? sees 141 vs 101/0. Fix is localised to test6.rs (write-error handling + SIGPIPE disposition), not to the container library.
